title: The Greatest Con Artists in History
description:
A Scot who sold a country that didn't exist, a butcher who claimed to be a lost heir, a Paris socialite with an empty safe, Andrew Carnegie's fake daughter, Charles Ponzi's 50% promise, the man who 'sold' the Eiffel Tower and the forger who fooled Hermann Göring. These are the true stories of history's greatest con artists, and where the legends get shaky, we say so.

Chapters are added automatically.

youtube_title: The Greatest Con Artists in History

beats.say: Paris, 1925. A man in a very nice suit invites a group of scrap metal dealers to one of the fanciest hotels in town.
Gentlemen, the government has a secret. The Eiffel Tower is falling apart.
So we are selling it. For scrap. Please, tell no one.
The whole tower? That's over seven thousand tons of iron!
And one of those dealers actually paid him. For a tower the man did not own.
Today, we meet history's greatest con artists: people who sold a tower they didn't own, a country that didn't exist, and fortunes that were never there.

show.text: The Greatest Con Artists in History

beats.say: London, 1822. A Scottish war hero named Gregor MacGregor arrives with amazing news.
He really had fought in South America's wars of independence against Spain. That part was true.
But now he said he was the prince of a country called Poyais, in Central America.
He even printed a guidebook. It described a capital city with a cathedral, an opera house and a bank.
Then he sold two hundred thousand pounds' worth of Poyais bonds. A bond is a loan: you pay now, and get paid back later with extra.

show.label: Poyais bonds sold in London, 1822
show.sub: a loan to a country that didn't exist

beats.say: Poyais also had a flag, a coat of arms and fancy army uniforms. All of it invented by MacGregor.
Hundreds of people signed up to move there. Many even swapped their savings for Poyais dollars, the fake country's own money, printed in Scotland.
Is there really an opera house?
My dear, the finest in the Americas.
In 1822 and 1823, about two hundred and fifty settlers sailed. When they landed in Honduras, there was no city. Only jungle.
Fever and hunger spread. About a hundred and eighty of them died. This part is no joke.
MacGregor then tried a similar scheme in France. He was put on trial in Paris, and walked free. He later retired in Venezuela on a general's pension.
And he kept promoting Poyais for years afterwards.
So one man sold a whole country, and the only real part was the jungle.
In 1854, a rich young Englishman, Roger Tichborne, sailed away and his ship was lost at sea.

tag.text: Roger Tichborne, heir to a fortune

beats.say: His mother, Lady Tichborne, refused to believe he was dead. She put ads in newspapers around the world.
In 1866, a butcher in Wagga Wagga, Australia, said he was the missing Roger.

tag.text: The butcher who said he was Roger

beats.say: Small problem. Roger was thin and grew up speaking French. The butcher was very heavy and spoke no French.
Still, in 1867 his mother met him in Paris, and said he was her son.
Roger! My boy!
Hello, Mother. Er, bonjour.
More than a hundred people who had known Roger backed him too. Others were sure he was a fraud.
The rest of the family said he was a fake, and the fight went to court in London.
This was Queen Victoria's Britain, and people followed the trials in the newspapers for years.
In 1874, a jury decided he was Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from London. He got fourteen years in prison for lying under oath.
So a butcher almost talked his way into a fortune, because a grieving mother wanted her son back.
Paris, the 1880s. Thérèse Humbert, a farm girl turned high society lady, says she has a secret fortune.
Her story: she saved an American millionaire, Robert Crawford, on a train. He left her a hundred million francs.
In her telling, she even climbed along the outside of the moving train to reach him. Very action movie.
But the fortune was locked in a safe, while a court fight over the will dragged on.
Meanwhile she lived like a queen, with a grand home on one of the smartest streets in Paris.
May I see the money, Madame?
It's in the safe. The court says nobody may open it.
Then please, take a loan. At a very nice rate.
And the twist: the rival heirs suing her, the Crawford nephews, were her own brothers in disguise.
For about twenty years, lenders handed her huge sums, all backed by a safe nobody could open.
In 1902, a court ordered the safe opened. Just before, the whole family vanished. They had fled to Spain.
The safe was nearly empty. Accounts differ, but one lists an old newspaper, a coin and a trouser button.

show.label: Inside the famous safe, 1902
show.sub: an old newspaper, a coin, a trouser button (accounts differ)

beats.say: They were caught in Madrid that December, and Thérèse got five years of hard labor.
So one locked safe fooled Paris for twenty years, and nobody ever got to look inside.
Cleveland, Ohio, the 1890s. Cassie Chadwick is the wife of a respected doctor, and she has a plan.
She hinted that she was the secret daughter of Andrew Carnegie, the steel king and one of the richest men alive.
The famous version says she let a lawyer watch her walk out of Carnegie's New York mansion, holding papers.
She carried notes, which are written promises to pay, signed "Andrew Carnegie". She had forged them.

objects.text: I PROMISE TO PAY — A. CARNEGIE

beats.say: Please keep this quiet. My father would be so embarrassed.
Of course. How much would Miss Carnegie like to borrow?
Bankers lent her huge sums. After all, who says no to Carnegie's daughter?
In 1904, one lender sued, and the whole thing fell apart. A small bank in Oberlin, Ohio, went bust.
Then Carnegie put out a statement that ended the fairy tale.
Mr. Carnegie does not know Mrs. Chadwick of Cleveland.

show.text: Mr. Carnegie does not know Mrs. Chadwick of Cleveland.

beats.say: Cassie was convicted in 1905 and died in prison two years later.
So a few forged signatures fooled whole banks, because nobody thought to ask Carnegie.
Boston, 1920. An Italian immigrant named Charles Ponzi has an offer that sounds amazing.
Give him your money, and in forty-five days you get it back, plus fifty percent.
His idea used postal reply coupons, little vouchers you could swap for stamps.
After World War One, they were cheap to buy in Italy, and worth more when traded in America.
On a tiny scale, that trick was real. But Ponzi mostly paid old investors with new investors' money.
Crowds lined up outside his office to hand over their savings.
Step right up! Everybody's getting rich!
In a few months, Ponzi went from nearly broke to a millionaire, with a mansion and a fancy car.
At his peak, about two hundred and fifty thousand dollars poured in every day.
Then the Boston Post newspaper did the math. He'd need a hundred and sixty million coupons. Only about twenty-seven thousand were actually out there.
Ponzi was arrested in August 1920, and the paper won a Pulitzer Prize for the story.
And today, paying old investors with new money has his name. It's called a Ponzi scheme.

show.title: The Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower

beats.say: Back to Paris. Victor Lustig was a con man from Austria-Hungary who liked to call himself a count.
He read a newspaper story saying the Eiffel Tower needed very expensive repairs.
So he faked government papers, and offered the tower for scrap. André Poisson, a dealer, paid.
Lustig fled to Vienna with the cash. Poisson was too embarrassed to go to the police.
So Lustig came back and tried it again! This time the dealer went to the police, and Lustig escaped.
A warning: most of these details come from a 1961 book by the Secret Service agent who helped catch him.
What's certain: in 1935, he was arrested in New York for printing fake money. Then he escaped jail on a rope of bedsheets!
Police caught him four weeks later. He ended up in Alcatraz, the famous island prison.
Back in 1920s New York, another con man, George C. Parker, was said to sell the Brooklyn Bridge. After many fraud convictions, he got life in prison in 1928.
The Netherlands, 1945. World War Two is over, and Dutch police arrest a painter named Han van Meegeren.
His crime? Selling a Vermeer, a painting by a famous Dutch master, to the top Nazi Hermann Göring.
Göring paid for it with a hundred and thirty-seven other paintings. Selling a Dutch treasure to the enemy could mean death.
It's not a Vermeer. I painted it myself!
He had painted on genuine old canvases, and baked his paint hard in an oven so it looked centuries old.
Nobody believed him. So, with witnesses watching, he painted a brand new fake Vermeer.
Experts then tested his paintings and agreed. He was convicted of forgery instead, and got one year. He died in 1947, before serving it.
So a man escaped a treason charge by proving he was a really good forger.
So what do all these con artists have in common? They sold people something they badly wanted to believe.
A new country. A lost son. A secret fortune. Easy money.
And even famous con stories can be shaky. Researchers have questioned many claims in Frank Abagnale's memoir, the book behind the movie "Catch Me If You Can".
So if it sounds too good to be true, ask to see inside the safe.
